The **University of Colorado Boulder** (**CU Boulder**,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-8)**CU**, or **Colorado**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Boulder, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulder,_Colorado "Boulder, Colorado"), United States. Founded in 1876, five months before [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado") became a [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federated_state "Federated state"), it is the [flagship university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship_university "Flagship university") of the [University of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado "University of Colorado") system. CU Boulder is a member of the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities"), is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-9) and has been referred to as a [Public Ivy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Ivy "Public Ivy").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-10)

The university consists of nine colleges and schools and offers over 150 academic programs, enrolling more than 35,000 students as of January 2022.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-11) In 2021, the university attracted the support of over $634 million for research and spent $536 million on research and development according to the [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"), ranking it 50th in the nation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-13) It receives the most NASA astrophysics technology grants of all academic institutions and is the only university in the world that has sent instruments to all planets in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-15)

The [Colorado Buffaloes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes "Colorado Buffaloes") compete in 17 varsity sports and are members of the [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I")[Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference"). The Buffaloes have won 28 national championships: 20 in [skiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Skiing_Championships "NCAA Skiing Championships"), 7 total in [men's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men's_Cross_Country_Championship "NCAA Men's Cross Country Championship") and [women's cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Cross_Country_Championship "NCAA Women's Cross Country Championship"), and 1 in [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes_football "Colorado Buffaloes football"). The university has produced [10 Olympic medalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_universities_with_Olympic_medals "List of American universities with Olympic medals"). Alumni, faculty, and researchers have included 12 [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") laureates[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-16) (of whom 5 were affiliated with the university when the prizes were awarded[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-18)), 10 [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") winners, 11 [MacArthur Fellows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellows "MacArthur Fellows"), 1 [Turing Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_Award "Turing Award") laureate, 20 [astronauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronauts "Astronauts") and 2 [associate justices of the United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_justices_of_the_United_States_Supreme_Court "Associate justices of the United States Supreme Court").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-22)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

On March 14, 1876, the Colorado territorial legislature passed an amendment to the state constitution that provided money for the establishment of the University of Colorado in Boulder, the [Colorado School of Mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_School_of_Mines "Colorado School of Mines") in [Golden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden,_Colorado "Golden, Colorado"), and the [Colorado Agricultural College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University "Colorado State University") in [Fort Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Collins "Fort Collins").

The cornerstone of the building that became Old Main was laid on September 20, 1875. The doors of the university opened on September 5, 1877. At the time, there were few [high schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_school "High school") in the state that could adequately prepare students for university work, so in addition to the university, a preparatory school was formed on campus. In the fall of 1877, the student body consisted of 15 students in the college proper and 50 students in the preparatory school. There were 38 men and 27 women, and their ages ranged from 12 to 23 years.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-23)

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Colorado was one of 131 colleges and universities nationally that took part in the [V-12 Navy College Training Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V-12_Navy_College_Training_Program "V-12 Navy College Training Program") which offered students a path to a navy commission.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-24)

CU hired its first female professor, [Mary Rippon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Rippon "Mary Rippon"), in 1878.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-25) It hired its first African-American professor, Charles H. Nilon, in 1956, and its first African-American librarian, [Mildred Nilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mildred_Nilon "Mildred Nilon"), in 1962.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-Boulder_Daily_Camera-2016-26) Its first African American female graduate, [Lucile Berkeley Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucile_Buchanan "Lucile Buchanan"), received her degree in 1918.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-KUSA-27)

## Campus

The CU Boulder campus

The main CU Boulder campus is located south of the [Pearl Street Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Street_Mall "Pearl Street Mall") and east of [Chautauqua Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chautauqua_Auditorium_(Boulder,_Colorado) "Chautauqua Auditorium (Boulder, Colorado)"). It consists of academic and residential buildings as well as research facilities. The East Campus is about a quarter-mile from the main campus and is composed mainly of athletic fields and research buildings. CU Boulder's campus has been ranked as one of the most beautiful college campuses in the United States by _[Travel + Leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel\_+\_Leisure "Travel + Leisure")_ and _[Condé Nast Traveler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cond%C3%A9\_Nast\_Traveler "Condé Nast Traveler")_.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-30)

### Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Architecture")]

CU Boulder's distinctive architecture style, known as Tuscan Vernacular Revival, was designed by architect [Charles Klauder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Klauder "Charles Klauder").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-Campus_Architect-31) The oldest buildings, such as Old Main (1876) and Macky Auditorium (1923), were in the [Collegiate Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Gothic "Collegiate Gothic") style of many East Coast schools, and Klauder's initial plans for the university's new buildings (approved in 1919) were in the same style.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-Campus_Architect-31) A month or so after approval, however, Klauder updated his design by sketching in a new wrap of rough, textured [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") walls with sloping, multi-leveled red-orange-[tiled roofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roof_tiles "Roof tiles") and [Indiana limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_limestone "Indiana limestone") trim.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-Campus_Architect-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-32) This formed the basis of a unified style, used in the design of fifteen other buildings between 1921 and 1939 and still followed on the campus to this day.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-Campus_Architect-31) The sandstone used in the construction of nearly all the buildings on campus was selected from a variety of [Front Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Range "Front Range") mountain quarries.

### Residence halls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Residence halls")]

Currently, freshmen and others attending the University of Colorado Boulder have an option of 24 on- and off-campus residence halls.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-33) Residence halls have 17 varieties of room types from singles to four-person rooms and others with apartment-style amenities.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-34) There are several communities of residence halls located throughout the campus, as well as in a separate area called Williams Village which is located approximately 1.5 miles off of the main campus. There is a free bus service that transports students to the main campus from Williams Village and vice versa. The university also offers Residential Academic Programs (RAPS) in many of its Residence Halls. RAPs provide students with in-dorm classes tailored to academic interests (international affairs, environmental studies, etc.).

### Engineering Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Engineering Center")]

The Engineering Center on the Northeast side of campus houses the nation's largest [geotechnical centrifuge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geotechnical_centrifuge_modeling "Geotechnical centrifuge modeling") as well as ion-implantation and microwave-propagation facilities, [spectrometers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_spectrometer "Optical spectrometer"), electron and other microscopes, and a structural analysis facility. ### Norlin Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Norlin Library")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Norlin_Library.jpg/250px-Norlin_Library.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Norlin_Library.jpg)

Norlin Library

Until 1903, the library collection was housed with the rest of the school in Old Main. The growing size of the library required a move, as the weight of the books was causing physical damage to the floor. The cornerstone for the first separate library building was laid in January 1903, and the building was opened in January 1904. When the new Norlin Library opened in 1940, the old library was turned over to the [Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre "Theatre") department and was converted into classrooms and a theatre.

Norlin Library was the last building to be designed by Klauder.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-36) There are two inscriptions on the western face of the building, overlooking the [Norlin Quadrangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norlin_Quadrangle_Historic_District "Norlin Quadrangle Historic District"). Both were composed by President Norlin. The larger inscription reads "Who knows only his own generation remains always a child," based on a [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero "Cicero") quotation, while the smaller inscription on the marble just over the door reads "Enter here the timeless fellowship of the human spirit."

### Macky Auditorium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Macky Auditorium")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Mackey_Auditorium_-_Colorado.jpg/250px-Mackey_Auditorium_-_Colorado.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mackey_Auditorium_-_Colorado.jpg)

Macky Auditorium

Macky Auditorium is a large building on the north edge of the University of Colorado campus, near 17th Street and University Avenue, which plays host to various talks, plays, and musical performances. Andrew J. Macky was a prominent businessman involved with the town of Boulder in the late 19th century. Macky served as the president, as well as a stockholder of the First National Bank, an institution founded by another early CU supporter, Lewis Cheney. Macky is credited with a number of landmarks throughout Boulder, where he was a carpenter and involved in politics.

The auditorium opened its doors in 1923, thirteen years after construction started. Macky's adopted daughter, May, sued for a third of Macky's estate, a case that took thirteen years to settle. May was angered that her father left her no money in his will, while leaving $300,000 to CU for the hall's construction. The university eventually won the case, and the majority of critical construction on the building resumed.

The building has a variety of architectural elements from various buildings around the globe that President [James Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Baker_(university_president) "James Baker (university president)"), CU's president at the turn of the 20th century, admired. The design of the auditorium is primarily [Neo-Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Gothic "Neo-Gothic"), with the primary materials being sandstone and red tile, like the rest of campus. The result is a unique building, with two large towers and sprawling ivy, that sets itself apart from the rest of the CU campus. Macky was refurbished in 1986, with improved seating, custom carpeting, modern plumbing, and an elevator. The towers' electronic bell system rings the hours during the day.

Macky is the home of two departments, both in the College of Music: the [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") Studies Department and the Choral Department. The lobby art gallery is open to patrons during performances, and to the general public at some other times during the week. The auditorium, with seating for 2,000, hosts almost all performances by the [Boulder Philharmonic Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulder_Philharmonic_Orchestra "Boulder Philharmonic Orchestra"), the Artist Series, and the CU Opera. Macky is also the home of many lectures, including the annual [Conference on World Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_on_World_Affairs "Conference on World Affairs") (CWA) opening keynote. In some recent past years, the venue has also hosted CWA panel discussions, Cinema Interruptus movie screenings and the popular jazz concert.

### University Memorial Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: University Memorial Center")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/University_of_Colorado_UMC_fountains_2006.jpg/250px-University_of_Colorado_UMC_fountains_2006.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Colorado_UMC_fountains_2006.jpg)

Dalton Trumbo Fountain Court behind the UMC on July 13, 2006

In 1947, Colorado Governor [Lee Knous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lee_Knous "William Lee Knous") issued a [proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation "Proclamation") to create a [memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial "Memorial") to Colorado's servicemen at the University of Colorado Boulder. A proposal to house this memorial in a [student union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_activity_center "Student activity center") building resulted in a remarkable fundraising effort. The University Memorial Center (UMC) opened its doors in October 1953 with President Robert Stearns presiding over the ribbon-cutting ceremony. The UMC quickly became the central landmark of the Boulder campus. A 1964 addition created a new bookstore, conference facilities, additional dining facilities, and offices to house the rapidly growing student activities and organizations. The expansion was financed through bonds granted by student fees.

The 1960s and '70s put the UMC at the center of student activism as students staged strikes, grape boycotts, love-ins, sit-ins, and walk-outs. The UMC Fountain Court (now the Dalton Trumbo Fountain Court) became a familiar sight to network television news watchers as the famous and notorious promoted their cause at CU Boulder. Entertainers as diverse as [Ramsey Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey_Lewis "Ramsey Lewis") and the [Grateful Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grateful_Dead "Grateful Dead") have performed in the [Glenn Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Miller "Glenn Miller") Ballroom. The UMC Connection, a student entertainment center in the basement, is a more informal gathering place, featuring pool tables and a small bowling alley. It also features Club 156, which hosts concerts from local and up-and-coming bands. In 1986, students passed another bond issue to remodel the food services area. The Alferd Packer Grill gets its name from [Alferd Packer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alferd_Packer "Alferd Packer"), a Colorado prospector accused of cannibalism.

### Center for Community

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Center for Community")]

The Center for Community, also known as the C4C by students, follows the distinct architecture guidelines of [Charles Klauder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Klauder "Charles Klauder") and is a 323,000-square-foot (30,000 m 2) facility[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-37) that is promised to be 20 percent to 25 percent more energy- and water-efficient compared to similar-sized buildings.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-dailycamera-38) The facility was completed in September 2010 at a cost of $84.4 million.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-39) The building is originally bond-financed through the CU treasurer and will be repaid through a combination of sources. A large portion of the debt, $47.4 million, will be repaid by Housing and Dining Services through room and board fees. Fees from Permit and Parking Services will contribute as well. The center also relies on $18 million in donations, a goal which has not been achieved, but has become a top fundraising priority for the university.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-dailycamera-38)

[![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/WeatherTechCafe.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WeatherTechCafe.jpg)

The Weather Tech Cafe

The building houses offices of Student Services, including [Campus Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campus_Card "Campus Card") Services, Disability Services, and Career Services, among others. These services have been relocated to the C4C from various locations around campus.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-dailycamera-38) For example, Career Services was previously housed in the basement of the Willard Dormitory. There is a 140,000-square-foot (13,000 m 2) underground parking structure that contains approximately 365 to 375 parking spaces.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-40) Student study areas are located on the upper floors and conference centers are open to campus and non-campus affiliates throughout the building.

#### Dining services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Dining services")]

The dining services offered within the C4C include a CU on the run "grab-n-go", The Bakery, a late-night dining hub called the Weather Tech Café, open until 2 A.M., and finally a central dining facility. This dining facility seats 900 and offers students up to nine specialty dining choices, including Persian, Asian, Latin, sushi, Italian, Kosher, a grill, salad bars, and desserts.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-41) Overall, the Dining Center is projected to serve around one million meals per year.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-dailycamera-38)

### Recreation Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Recreation Center")]

In 1973 the student recreation center was built on the CU Boulder's main campus, by the architect James Wallace.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-42) The funding to build the recreation center came entirely from student fees, which also funded the expansions in 1990 and 2014. The recreation center features strength and cardio space, basketball/volleyball courts, the only ice rink in Boulder proper, lap pool, dive well, fitness studios (cycling, rowing, etc.), climbing gym, turf gym, and an iconic[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] outdoor pool in the shape of the CU Boulder buffalo mascot. It is currently about 300,000 square feet (28,000 m 2) and operates on a $5 million annual budget. The center is co-managed by the division of student affairs and CUSG, CU Boulder's student government. It is located on the northern edge of campus next to [Folsom Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folsom_Field "Folsom Field"). It is open seven days a week and on average 16 hours a day, with most of its facilities available for use during those hours.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-43)

The Mary Rippon Theatre is an outdoor [theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theater "Theater") and the site of many [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural "Cultural") events, notably the [Colorado Shakespeare Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Shakespeare_Festival "Colorado Shakespeare Festival"). Old Main is the oldest building on campus, and previously served as the Medical School for the University of Colorado system.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-45)

### Galleries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Galleries")]

Norlin Library features two art galleries, several dedicated art spaces, and artworks on display throughout the building. The CU Art Museum features works of modern and contemporary art, as well as historical artworks. The Museum's permanent collection includes over 5,000 works of art from numerous time periods and cultures. The UMC Art Gallery exhibits a variety of visual offerings ranging from student works created on campus to presentations of internationally recognized artists. Andrew J. Macky Gallery showcases the work of both local and national artists and is housed in the historic Macky Auditorium.

### Museums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Museums")]

[University of Colorado Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Museum_of_Natural_History "University of Colorado Museum of Natural History") has one of the most extensive natural history collections in the Rocky Mountain and Plains regions, representing the disciplines of anthropology, botany, entomology, paleontology, and zoology. It is located in the Henderson building, named after its first curator, Judge [Junius Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junius_Henderson "Junius Henderson"), and hosts the Museum and Field Studies master's (MS) program. The CU Heritage Center[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-46) tells the stories of CU Boulder's past and present and is housed in Old Main, the first building constructed on campus. Seven galleries exhibit art and memorabilia associated with CU faculty and alumni. The [Fiske Planetarium and Science Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiske_Planetarium "Fiske Planetarium") features a 60 ft (18 m). planetarium dome and produces laser shows, live concerts, and an ongoing series of public programs. Fiske also offers a hands-on science museum with interactive exhibits and space-themed art.

### Performing arts facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Performing arts facilities")]

The University of Colorado Boulder College of Music presents over 400 performances and educational events bringing together faculty, students, and guest artists each year through the Pendulum New Music Series. They present musical genres including classical, jazz, world music, and new music. The University of Colorado Boulder Department of Theatre & Dance is home to the Charlotte York Irey Dance Theatre, the University Theatre, and the Loft Theatre, as well as Grusin Music Hall and the Chamber Music Hall in the [College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Music "College of Music"). More than twenty productions are presented each year, featuring student and faculty actors, dancers, choreographers, directors, and designers, as well as the work of professional guest artists. Student work is also showcased in the annual CU Boulder Fringe Festival, produced by OnStage, a student performing arts group.

The University of Colorado Boulder is divided into several colleges and schools. While the college of [Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts "Arts") and [Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences "Sciences") is by far the largest, the university also consists of the college of [Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering") and Applied Science, the Program in Environmental Design, [Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"), [Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music"), [Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"), the [Leeds School of Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_School_of_Business "Leeds School of Business"), and the College of Communication, Media, Design and Information. Most, if not all, of these colleges and schools also incorporate master's- and doctoral-level degree programs. At the university, there are currently approximately 3,400 courses available in over 150 disciplines, making up 85 majors ranging from Accounting to Women's Studies.

[University of Colorado Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Law_School "University of Colorado Law School") is the smallest and most selective of the colleges. The Wolf Law Building, the new home of the Law School, was dedicated on September 8, 2006, by [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court "United States Supreme Court") justice [Stephen Breyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Breyer "Stephen Breyer").

The [Leeds School of Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_School_of_Business "Leeds School of Business") has an enrollment of 3,300 students, including undergraduates, master's candidates, and Ph.D. candidates. The undergraduate program ranks 39th in the country and the undergraduate entrepreneurship program ranks 14th in the nation. The MBA program ranks 26th among all public universities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The faculty are ranked 38th in the nation according to the _Academy of Management Journal_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

CU Boulder adopted an [honor code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_honor_code "Academic honor code") in 2000 following growing concerns about [academic dishonesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_dishonesty "Academic dishonesty") on campus in the late 1990s.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-56) A copy of the code stating "On my honor, as a University of Colorado Boulder student, I have neither given nor received unauthorized assistance on this work" is engraved on a metal plate and posted in every classroom on campus.

Undergraduates who seek an academic challenge may participate in CU's Honors Program. Begun in 1931, the Honors Program currently consists of the top ten percent of incoming freshmen and participating undergraduates with a 3.3 GPA or greater (on a 4.0 scale). The program offers over 40 honors classes each semester, taught by tenured or tenure-track professors and limited to class sizes of 17[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-57) students. Honors students also have the opportunity to graduate with honors, high honors, and highest honors, by writing and defending a thesis during their senior year. The program extends into the residence halls through the Kittredge Honors Program. The Presidents Leadership Class is a program for top scholars at the University of Colorado Boulder. Scholars participate in a four-year leadership development program. The program provides opportunities to the top fifty students at CU from every major and discipline.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-58)

One option for students (mostly freshmen and sophomores) living on campus is to join a residential academic program (RAP). Each RAP focuses on a curricular theme and offers courses in the residence hall itself. The programs also include educational activities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Center for Advanced Engineering and Technology Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Center for Advanced Engineering and Technology Education")]

The Center for Advanced Engineering and Technology Education (CAETE) is a partnership between the College of Engineering and Applied Science and the Division of Continuing Education and Professional Studies at the University of Colorado Boulder. As the [distance learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_learning "Distance learning") and professional studies arm of the College of Engineering and Applied Science, CAETE provides courses from the college to working professionals via the Internet and CD-ROM. Students can take courses for professional development or toward earning a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") or graduate certificate (in some disciplines) in [aerospace engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering"), [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_at_Boulder_Computer_Science_Department "University of Colorado at Boulder Computer Science Department"), [electrical, computer and energy engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_engineering "Electrical engineering"), [engineering management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_management "Engineering management"), and [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications "Telecommunications"). Founded in 1983, CAETE currently receives over 1,000 enrollments a year from over 250 job sites in [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), across the nation, and abroad.

### University of Colorado Engineering Management Program

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: University of Colorado Engineering Management Program")]

The University of Colorado Engineering Management Program (formally the Lockheed Martin Engineering Management Program) is a graduate and undergraduate-level initiative within the College of Engineering and Applied Science at the University of Colorado Boulder. It was initiated in 1987 with an endowment from [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin") to meet the needs of the high-tech industry in [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado").

The _[CU Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CU\_Independent "CU Independent")_ is the award-winning, student-run news publication for the University of Colorado Boulder.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-:0-70) It has been digital-only since August 2006, one of the first major college newspapers to drop its print edition.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-:0-70) It was founded in 1978 as the _Working Press_ but soon adopted the name _Campus Press._ It was launched by Mal Deans, a CU journalism instructor, to serve as a student-run newspaper after the _[Colorado Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado\_Daily "Colorado Daily")_ left campus and became a community newspaper.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-71) The name was changed to the _CU Independent_ in August 2008 after it split from the journalism school's curriculum in the wake of a controversy over a student journalist's racially charged column.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-72) In December 2019, the university's media college, which had been providing space and retaining staff pay, announced it would defund the _CU Independent_ in favor of a faculty-led media enterprise. Staff of the _CU Independent_ said they would continue to maintain the website and publish content under a new funding model separate from the college.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-73)

The blog is created and edited by Andrew D. Chapman, a philosophy lecturer at this university.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-77) The essays generally include references or sources for more information.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-78)

_What's Wrong?_ is the "not quite official" blog of the University of Colorado, Boulder's Center for Values and Social Policy. The blog's purpose is to provide "a forum for discussing and reporting on topics in applied normative philosophy".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-80)

### Research institutes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Research institutes")]

CU Boulder's research mission is supported by 11 research institutes within the university. Each research institute supports faculty from multiple academic departments, allowing institutes to conduct truly multidisciplinary research.

The Institute for Behavioral Genetics (IBG) is a research institute within the Graduate School dedicated to conducting and facilitating research on the genetic and environmental bases of individual differences in behavior.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-81) After its [founding in 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_E._McClearn "Gerald E. McClearn") IBG led the resurging interest in genetic influences on behavior. IBG was the first post-World War II research institute dedicated to research in [behavioral genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavioral_genetics "Behavioral genetics"). IBG remains one of the top research facilities for research in [behavioral genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavioral_genetics "Behavioral genetics"), including [human behavioral genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_behavioral_genetics "Human behavioral genetics"), [psychiatric genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_genetics "Psychiatric genetics"), [quantitative genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_genetics "Quantitative genetics"), [statistical genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_genetics "Statistical genetics"), and animal behavioral genetics.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-82)

The Institute of Cognitive Science (ICS) at CU Boulder promotes interdisciplinary research and training in cognitive science. ICS is highly interdisciplinary; its research focuses on [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"), [language processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_processing "Language processing"), [emotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion "Emotion"), and higher-level cognition using experimental methods. It is home to a state-of-the-art [fMRI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMRI "FMRI") system used to collect [neuroimaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroimaging "Neuroimaging") data.

ATLAS Institute is a center for interdisciplinary research and academic study, where engineering, computer science and robotics are blended with design-oriented topics.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-83) Part of CU Boulder's College of Engineering and Applied Science, the institute offers academic programs at the undergraduate, master's and doctoral levels, and administers research labs, hacker and makerspaces, and a black box experimental performance studio. At the beginning of the 2018–2019 academic year, approximately 1,200 students were enrolled in ATLAS academic programs and the institute sponsored six research labs.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-84)

In addition to IBG, ICS and ATLAS, the university's other institutes include Biofrontiers Institute, [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_Institute_for_Research_in_Environmental_Sciences "Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences"), Institute of [Arctic & Alpine Research (INSTAAR)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Arctic_and_Alpine_Research "Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research"), Institute of Behavioral Science (IBS), CU Boulder-[NIST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NIST "NIST") joint institute [JILA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JILA "JILA"), [Laboratory for Atmospheric & Space Physics (LASP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory_for_Atmospheric_and_Space_Physics "Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics"), Renewable & Sustainable Energy Institute (RASEI), and the [University of Colorado Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Museum_of_Natural_History "University of Colorado Museum of Natural History").

The [University of Colorado Student Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Student_Government "University of Colorado Student Government") (CUSG) is the student government for the University of Colorado Boulder. The government contains three branches: executive, legislative, and judicial. Presiding officers for the student government are elected in a bi-annual vote administered to the 30,000 students at the university. The student government has an autonomy agreement with the University Administration and oversees an annual budget of $36.6 million. CUSG is responsible for the management of the University Student Union, the Recreation Center, the LGBTQ Resource Center, the Women's Resource Center, and the Wardenburg Health Center, along with various other facilities on campus. The government also oversees the fiscal appropriations of over 120 student groups on a yearly basis.

### CU Gaming and Esports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: CU Gaming and Esports")]

Founded in December 2015,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-88) CU Gaming is the University of Colorado's largest student organization with over 3,500 current members. The organization offers biweekly and monthly [gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Video_games "Category:Video games") events for its members as well as the general student population at CU.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-89) CU Gaming offers leadership, career, and internship opportunities for members who are interested in working in the gaming and [esports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esports "Esports") industries.

CU Esports, CU Gaming's sister organization, fields over a dozen teams in a variety of games. In November 2020, CU Esports' [Valorant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valorant "Valorant") Black Team was crowned the Collegiate Valorant Conference Fall 2020 Series Champions after defeating [UCF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCF "UCF") Esports 2–1 in the finals.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Hiking Club

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Hiking Club")]

Founded in May 1919, the [Hiking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiking "Hiking") Club is the longest running student organization at the University of Colorado Boulder.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-CU_Hiking_Club-90) It is a non-profit, student-run organization for university students and affiliates interested in hiking and outdoors activities, with hundreds of active members on campus.

Boulder Freeride is the ski and snowboard club at the University of Colorado Boulder. It was started in 1933. Boulder Freeride is active year-round. Boulder Freeride organizes a number of ski trips each year. ### CU Cycling Club

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: CU Cycling Club")]

Founded in 1983 by Jim Castagneri, the [cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport") team was taken to the national championships in 1987 by 1992 Olympian [John Stenner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stenner "John Stenner"). The CU cycling team frequently ranks in the top five [USA Cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Cycling "USA Cycling") Collegiate teams in both [road cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_bicycle_racing "Road bicycle racing") and [mountain biking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_biking "Mountain biking") disciplines. They have won the national championship on several occasions, including 2005, when they won in both disciplines.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-94) Many members of the club have gone on into professional cycling, including [Sepp Kuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepp_Kuss "Sepp Kuss") and [Tyler Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler_Hamilton "Tyler Hamilton").

A founding club member of the Rocky Mountain Collegiate Cycling Conference,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-95) the team is open to any student who pays annual dues and meets a minimum amount of credits during the semester. The members include nearly every different type of cyclist, from [BMX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMX "BMX") riders, [trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_bike_trials "Mountain bike trials"), and [bicycle commuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_commuting "Bicycle commuting") to elite amateur or part-time professional road and mountain riders. Specifically, to qualify for road or mountain nationals, a rider must have enough high race results to upgrade to "A" category in the USA Cycling rankings. A number of "A" riders will be chosen by the coaches to represent CU at the National Championships. The number of riders the team is allowed to send is based on how well the team did overall during the season.

### Volunteer Resource Center

The Volunteer Resource Center is a student-funded organization aimed at promoting volunteerism in the Boulder community. They provide a database with volunteer opportunities of 250 organizations around campus and in the Boulder area.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-About_VRC-98) The CU Boulder campus was recently one of 3 U.S. Universities to receive the Presidential Award for Exemplary Student Community Service in 2008. The Volunteer Resource Center hosts or participates in special volunteer events and activities, including Alternative Breaks, Better Boulder Better World, and The Buffalo Can Challenge. The Volunteer Resource Center is also a yearly Volunteer Internship Program, which engages six selected students through an interview process to create events aimed at involving more freshmen in volunteering, effectively managing all logistics of the event, and implementing the events on campus.

### Greek life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Greek life")]

The [Panhellenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_fraternities_and_sororities "College fraternities and sororities") sorority community consists of roughly a dozen chapters. The men's fraternities at the University of Colorado are not officially affiliated with the school; however, they are still a presence on campus. About 13% of the undergraduate student body participates in Greek life.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-99) The Multicultural Greek Council acts as a liaison between the member organizations and university administration.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-100)

The death of Chi Psi pledge Gordie Bailey from alcohol poisoning during hazing in 2004 caused Boulder fraternities to reorganize and sever legal affiliation to the university. Students gathered for a candlelight vigil for the deceased football player on the Boulder campus on September 20, 2004.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-101)

### Left Right TIM Improv Comedy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Left Right TIM Improv Comedy")]

Started in 2008 by CU-Boulder students,[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-102) Left Right TIM is the Boulder area's premier and longest-running improv comedy team, performing a weekly improvised comedy show every Friday during the university's academic year in the Hale Anthropology Building Room 270 of the school's campus. The team has performed in cities around the country as well as opening for established stand-up comedians and improv theaters.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-103)[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

## Sports, clubs, and traditions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Sports, clubs, and traditions")]

Sports teams at the school are called Buffaloes. The [varsity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varsity_team "Varsity team") athletic teams participate in the [NCAA's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association")[Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") ([FBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_Bowl_Subdivision "Football Bowl Subdivision") for football, see [Bowl Championship Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowl_Championship_Series "Bowl Championship Series")) as a member of the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference"). The school rejoined the Big 12 in 2024, ending its affiliation with the [Pac-12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac-12_Conference "Pac-12 Conference"). (CU had previously been a member of the former [Big Eight Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Eight_Conference "Big Eight Conference"), whose members had merged with four schools of the former [Southwest Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Conference "Southwest Conference") to create the new Big 12 Conference in 1996.) The official school colors are silver and gold, as opposed to the common belief of black and gold. Silver and gold were chosen to represent the state's mineral wealth, but the colors did not look good together on the uniforms, so black was substituted.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-104) There are three official fight songs: "Glory Colorado", "Go Colorado", and "Fight CU."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-105)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-106) In the early 1980s, the Board of Regents changed the school colors to sky blue and gold; but the changed proved highly unpopular with students and alumni, and the colors were changed back after 1985.

In 1934, the university teams were officially nicknamed the "Buffaloes." Previous [nicknames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_nickname "Athletic nickname") used by the press included the "Silver Helmets" and "Frontiersmen." The final game of 1934, against the [University of Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Pioneers "Denver Pioneers"), saw the first running of a buffalo in a Colorado football game. A buffalo calf was rented from a local ranch and ran along the sidelines.

### Varsity athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: Varsity athletics")]

Main article: [Colorado Buffaloes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes "Colorado Buffaloes")

CU's varsity teams have won national championships in [skiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Skiing_Championships "NCAA Skiing Championships"), [men's cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men's_Cross_Country_Championship "NCAA Men's Cross Country Championship"), [women's cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Cross_Country_Championship "NCAA Women's Cross Country Championship"), and [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_FBS_national_football_championship "NCAA Division I FBS national football championship"). Conference championships have also been won in several sports. Several club sports, such as cycling, swimming & diving, and triathlon, have won national championships in addition to the varsity teams.

In football, CU enjoys an in-state rivalry with the [Colorado State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State "Colorado State")[Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Rams_football "Colorado State Rams football") in the "[Rocky Mountain Showdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountain_Showdown "Rocky Mountain Showdown")", a game that was formerly played at the neutral site [Empower Field at Mile High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empower_Field_at_Mile_High "Empower Field at Mile High") in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"). Additionally, Colorado and former Big Eight and Big 12 rival [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nebraska%E2%80%93Lincoln "University of Nebraska–Lincoln")[Cornhuskers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska_Cornhuskers_football "Nebraska Cornhuskers football") have played some notable games, often finishing their respective seasons in nationally televised confrontations on the Friday following [Thanksgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving_(United_States) "Thanksgiving (United States)") since the 1990s. This ended after the 2010 season as a result of CU joining the Pac-12 and Nebraska joining the [Big Ten Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference"). The team has seen renewed success since 2023 with former NFL star [Deion Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deion_Sanders "Deion Sanders") as head coach.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-Sports_Illustrated-107)

### Mascot and spirit program

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=42 "Edit section: Mascot and spirit program")]

See also: [Colorado Buffaloes §Mascots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes#Mascots "Colorado Buffaloes")

CU also includes a spirit program. The spirit program consists of three teams: two cheerleading squads and the CU Express Dance Team. The cheerleading program consists of a competitive co-ed squad as well as a competitive all-girl squad. Both the cheerleading squad and the Express Dance Team compete at NCA/NDA College Nationals. In 2007, the cheerleading squad finished sixth[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-108) at NCA Nationals in [Daytona Beach, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytona_Beach,_Florida "Daytona Beach, Florida"). All squads support the home games of [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes_football "Colorado Buffaloes football"), Women's Basketball, Men's Basketball, and Women's Volleyball teams, along with other athletic and social events.

The school's live mascot is a female [American bison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison "American bison") named [Ralphie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralphie_the_Buffalo "Ralphie the Buffalo").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-109) The costumed mascot CHIP is also a part of the CU Spirit Program. CHIP is a costumed buffalo that represents the University of Colorado at numerous athletic and social events. Along with the Cheer and Dance Program, CHIP competes on a national level once a year against mascots from around the country, including [Bucky Badger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucky_Badger "Bucky Badger"), [Sparty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparty "Sparty"), [Aubie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubie "Aubie"), [Goldy Gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher "Goldy Gopher") and many other [Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot_Hall_of_Fame "Mascot Hall of Fame") mascots. Most recently, CHIP competed in the 2009 UCA national competition and was crowned #1 and the national champion after performing a skit titled "CHIP's Favorite Video Games".

### Clubs and other organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=43 "Edit section: Clubs and other organizations")]

CU Boulder offers a variety of political student organizations that cover the full spectrum of politics. Among them are Amnesty International, which focuses on human rights worldwide, Model United Nations (MUN), which simulates the UN with a focus on international relations and diplomacy, as well as the College Democrats and the College Republicans. The University of Colorado also offers many clubs promoting diversity and human rights, such as the Gay Straight Alliance. Students can also choose from a plethora of clubs and organizations centered on ethnicities and countries, as well as different religious groups. CU Boulder also maintains one of the nation's most competitive student-run parliamentary debate programs. In 2010, CU Boulder became the first fully student-run program to win the [National Parliamentary Tournament of Excellence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parliamentary_Tournament_of_Excellence "National Parliamentary Tournament of Excellence") (NPTE).[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-110)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Colorado_Boulder&action=edit&section=44 "Edit section: Demographics")]

As of fall 2021, there were 35,897 students enrolled. 66.2 percent of the student population identified as white. 56.9% were Colorado residents and 10.1% were California residents.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-111) A 2014 survey found that 16.3% of the students were registered as members of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), along with 10.5% of CU Boulder non-faculty staff and 6% of CU Boulder faculty.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder#cite_note-112)

*   Average net price is generated by subtracting the average amount of federal, state/local government, or institutional grant or scholarship aid from the total cost of attendance.Total cost of attendance is the sum of published tuition and required fees (lower of in-district or in-state), books and supplies, and the weighted average for Food and Housing and other expenses.

*   Beginning students are those who are entering postsecondary education for the first time.

*   Title IV aid to students includes grant aid, work study aid, and loan aid. These include: Federal Pell Grants, Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants (FSEOG), Teacher Education Assistance for College and Higher Education (TEACH) Grants, Federal Work-Study, Subsidized Direct Loans, and Unsubsidized Direct Loans. For those Title IV recipients, net price is reported by income category and includes students awarded federal aid even if none of that aid was provided in the form of grants. While Title IV status defines the cohort of student for which the data are reported, the definition of net price remains the same – total cost of attendance minus grant aid.

Overall Graduation Rate and Transfer-Out Rate

The overall graduation rate is also known as the "Student Right to Know" or IPEDS graduation rate. It tracks the progress of students who began their studies as **full-time, first-time degree- or certificate-seeking students** to see if they complete a degree or other award such as a certificate within 150% of "normal time" for completing the program in which they are enrolled.

Some institutions also report a transfer-out rate, which is the percentage of the full-time, first-time students who transferred to another institution without completing at the current institution.

Note that not all students at the institution are tracked for these rates. Students who have already attended another postsecondary institution, or who began their studies on a part-time basis, are not tracked for this rate. **At this institution, 73 percent of entering students were counted as "full-time, first-time" in 2024.**

These measures are also reported for students receiving Pell grants and those students that do not receive Pell grants. These measures provide the 8-year award-completion rates by award level (certificates, associate's and bachelor degrees) after entering an institution. For students who did not earn any undergraduate award after 8-years of entry, the enrollment statuses are reported as either still enrolled at the institution, or subsequently transferred out of the institution. Unlike the Graduation Rates data, all reporting institutions must report on their transfer outs regardless if the institution has a mission that provides substantial transfer preparation.
